spec.premise: a baker's hands at four in the morning
a girl returns to her grandmother's island to sell a boat

set.title: The Low Water Year
set.headnote: The following passage is from the novel The Low Water Year (1957) by Teodora Hallsey. Agnes, nineteen, has been sent from the mainland to the island where her grandmother once lived.

characters: Agnes Rune, nineteen, raised partly on the island, now living on the mainland; sent by her grandmother to sell the family boat
Hedda Rune, Agnes's grandmother, bedridden in a mainland home, absent from the scene but directing it by letter
Osk Pell, an island neighbor in his sixties, buyer of the boat, former creditor of Agnes's grandfather
blueprint.setting: Scarrow Island, a small northern fishing island reached by ferry, late autumn in the 1950s; the shingle beach, the boat shed, the hauled-out boat Linnet; the mainland visible as a gray line across the water
blueprint.situation: Agnes arrives on the morning ferry with a pre-written bill of sale and instructions not to haggle and not to go up to the house. Pell names an absurdly low price, then reveals that Hedda set it herself to repay an old debt disguised as a sale.
blueprint.conflict: Agnes believes she is performing a plain transaction on her own authority; she discovers she is the instrument of her grandmother's arrangement with Pell, and must decide whether to obey the instruction to stay away from the house and catch the afternoon ferry.
blueprint.central_idea: Acts of settling accounts between the old are carried out through the young, who discover that what looked like their own errand was someone else's unfinished business; the recognition of being used is also a recognition of belonging.
blueprint.complexity: Hedda's manipulation is both a humiliation of Agnes and a kind of trust; Pell's acceptance of an unfair price in his favor is also an act of loyalty to a dead man and a proud woman; Agnes's final disobedience (going up to the house, missing the ferry) is simultaneously a rejection of being used and a deeper acceptance of her place in the family's accounts. The boat, sold for nothing, is worth more to everyone than its price.

devices.quote: like something that had not agreed to be walked on
devices.function: Figures the island shingle as resisting Agnes's return, establishing her estrangement and the island's indifference to her errand

devices.quote: like a scar that had decided to stay
devices.function: The replaced plank becomes a healed wound with its own will, tying the boat to family history and to the stubbornness that governs the sale

devices.quote: a face the weather had been at for sixty years
devices.function: Weather becomes an unfinished craftsman working on Pell, marking him as shaped by the island and suggesting incompleteness, the way the debt is unfinished

devices.quote: the plain thing had a hole in it
devices.function: Agnes's simple plan is figured as a leaking hull, letting cold in; links her inner disturbance to the boat and foreshadows the bailer

devices.quote: You sold a boat; you took the money
devices.function: Agnes's brisk mental script in second-person generalities exposes her wish for the errand to be impersonal, which the scene denies

devices.quote: She remembered Hedda in the stern
devices.function: Inserts the image of Hedda refusing to let the boat go anywhere before Pell explains the price, so his explanation confirms rather than surprises

devices.quote: the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead
devices.function: Charon's fee frames the sale as a passage toward death and the money as funeral payment; the inversion (the ferryman paying) captures Agnes's confusion about who is giving and who is taking

devices.quote: She wants it to look like a sale.
devices.function: The sale that Agnes came to perform is revealed as a disguise for a repayment, undercutting the title act of the passage

devices.quote: it did not change the shape of her hand
devices.function: The money's triviality is registered physically rather than announced, flattening the climax into a wry, bodily fact
Compressed sibilants give Pell a solid, deliberate sound matching his unhurried conduct
The fragment insists on Pell's lifelong exclusion from the boat, hinting at the unpaid debt before it is spoken

devices.quote: There's a bailer in the kitchen
devices.function: The bailer Hedda removed so Pell would not get it symbolizes what she withholds even while giving; carrying it to her becomes the task Agnes chooses over the one assigned

devices.quote: he did not help her, and he did not hurry
devices.function: Pell's deliberateness against Agnes's haste in city shoes defines her as the outsider and him as the island's tempo

devices.quote: Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.
devices.function: The sentence turns from brisk transaction to rueful recognition of being used, redirecting the passage toward Agnes's choice

devices.quote: the stones rolled the same as before
devices.function: Returns the opening image with Agnes's altered relation to it: the ground has not changed, her hurry has

devices.quote: There isn't a price to argue.
devices.function: Pell's flat refusal to bargain signals that the transaction is not economic, before he explains why

shifts.quote: Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.
shifts.from: Agnes as brisk agent of a plain transaction
shifts.to: Agnes as instrument of her grandmother's arrangement, rueful and newly aware

shifts.quote: let the four o'clock leave without her
shifts.from: Compliance with Hedda's instructions and the plan to leave
shifts.to: Deliberate disobedience and lingering, accepting the island's slower time

blueprint.speaker: Third-person limited narrator aligned with Agnes; access to her memories and thoughts but not Pell's or Hedda's
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs of prose; clipped dialogue; one flashback paragraph; closing paragraph returns to the opening shingle image.

provenance.note: Original passage written for practice purposes; invented author, title, island and characters.

stanzas: The ferry put Agnes off at Scarrow at eleven, and
she walked up from the slip with her grandmother's house
key in one glove and the bill of sale, already made out,
in the other. She had been told not to go up to the
house. "There is nothing in it you want," Hedda had said
from the bed in the mainland home, "and if you go in you
will start wanting." So Agnes turned left along the
shingle toward the boat shed instead, in city shoes, the
stones rolling under her like something that had not
agreed to be walked on.
The Linnet lay keel-down on her cradle where she had
been hauled in October, and she looked smaller than
Agnes remembered, the way the island did, the way the
dock did; only the sky had kept its size. Someone had
put a tarpaulin over her and weighted it with four
stones, one at each corner, exactly. Agnes knew who. Osk
Pell did everything in fours. He came down the path from
his own place while she was still working the first
stone loose, and he did not help her, and he did not
hurry.
"You'll be Hedda's girl," he said. He was a square,
slow, salt-cured man with a face the weather had been at
for sixty years and had not finished. "She wrote me you
were coming. She wrote me what to pay." "She told me not
to argue the price." "There isn't a price to argue." He
named it. It was less than her train fare had been.
Agnes looked at the hull, at the strake her grandfather
had replaced the summer she was nine, the new wood still
a shade paler, like a scar that had decided to stay.
"That boat is worth ten times that," she said. "You know
it is." "I know it is."
She had come to do a plain thing. You sold a boat;
you took the money; you caught the four o'clock back.
Now the plain thing had a hole in it and she could feel
the cold coming through. She remembered Hedda in the
stern with the tiller under her arm like a parcel she
had no intention of giving up, not steering so much as
declining to let the boat go anywhere else. She
remembered Osk Pell on the dock those summers, never
once in the boat. Never once.
"Your grandfather owed me for the engine," Pell
said. "Nineteen thirty-eight. He never paid it and I
never asked, and your grandmother never forgot it.
That's the price. She's paying the debt. She wants it to
look like a sale." He took the stones off the other
three corners himself now, one, two, three, setting each
on the shingle as if it might be needed again. "If I'd
offered her a fair price she'd have refused it. She'd
have let the boat rot sooner than take money from me."
Agnes thought of the coin you were supposed to put
in the mouth of the dead for the ferryman, and how the
stories never said what happened if the ferryman was the
one who paid. Across the water the mainland was a gray
line with the home somewhere on it, a window, a bed, a
woman who had arranged the whole morning from under a
blanket and sent her granddaughter to stand in the wind
and be the hands of it. Agnes had thought she was the
one doing the selling. She signed the bill of sale on
the Linnet's gunwale, pressing hard so the pencil would
take on the damp paper, and Pell counted the money into
her glove, and it was so little that it did not change
the shape of her hand.
"Go up to the house," Pell said. "She told you not
to. Go anyway. There's a bailer in the kitchen she took
off the boat so I wouldn't get it. It's got her initials
in it. Take it to her." Agnes did not answer. She walked
back along the shingle, and the stones rolled the same
as before, but she had the time now to let them, and at
the turn where the path went up to the house instead of
down to the slip, she stood for a while and let the four
o'clock leave without her.

items.stem: The contrast between Agnes working at the stone and Pell, who "did not help her, and he did not hurry" ([[r1]]), primarily emphasizes

options.text: Agnes's eagerness to finish an errand on an island whose pace she no longer shares
options.label: correct
options.why: Agnes in city shoes hurrying to work the stone loose, set against Pell's deliberate approach, marks her as the outsider moving at mainland speed; the passage later confirms this when she lets the ferry leave and has 'the time now' to let the stones roll.

options.text: Pell's resentment toward a family that has excluded him from the boat for decades
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Pell's slowness is characteristic ('did everything in fours'), and nothing in his conduct or speech expresses resentment; he later acts with loyalty to Hedda.

options.text: Agnes's physical weakness compared with a man hardened by sixty years of weather
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Reads the scene as a test of strength; the stones are not described as heavy, and the contrast concerns tempo and manner, not capability.

options.text: Pell's refusal to acknowledge Agnes as the rightful seller of her grandmother's boat
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell immediately recognizes her as 'Hedda's girl' and proceeds with the sale; he does not dispute her role, though he knows Hedda set the terms.

items.stem: A student claims that Hedda controls the sale despite her absence from the island. Which of the following sentences of commentary most clearly links the phrase "arranged the whole morning from under a blanket" ([[r1]]) to that claim?

options.text: The sentence pairs a verb of command with an image of confinement, showing that Hedda's authority survives the loss of her mobility.
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly connects the evidence ('arranged' against 'under a blanket') to the claim about control despite absence; the passage supports it with Hedda's letters to Pell and instructions to Agnes.

options.text: The sentence describes Hedda lying in bed at the home, which proves she is too ill to travel to the island herself to sell the boat.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Explains Hedda's absence rather than her control; it restates the circumstance without connecting to the claim's main point.

options.text: The sentence shows that Agnes resents being sent into the wind, which establishes the conflict between the two generations of the family.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Shifts focus from Hedda's control to Agnes's resentment and generational conflict, which the quoted phrase does not itself address.

options.text: The sentence uses the word 'blanket' to suggest that Hedda is hiding something from Agnes, which the reader learns is the debt owed to Pell.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Over-reads 'blanket' as concealment; the text uses it for physical confinement, and the hidden debt is Pell's revelation, not the point of this phrase.

refs.quote: arranged the whole morning from under a blanket

evidence_quotes: a woman who had arranged the whole morning from under a blanket

items.stem: The placement of Pell's reply "I know it is." ([[r1]]) immediately after Agnes's protest serves primarily to

options.text: signal that the price is not a matter of the boat's value, before the reason is given
options.label: correct
options.why: By conceding her point at once, Pell removes value from the dispute; the reader is left with an unexplained gap that the fifth paragraph fills.

options.text: show that Pell has been shamed by Agnes into reconsidering the sum he has named
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell does not alter the price; his agreement is calm and the sum remains unchanged through the signing.

options.text: reveal that Pell doubts whether Hedda truly intended the boat to be sold to him
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in Pell's words suggests doubt about Hedda's intent; he cites her letters as authoritative.

options.text: suggest that Agnes has inherited her grandmother's skill at bargaining for a fair price
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The exchange ends bargaining rather than displaying it, and Hedda is shown refusing money, not bargaining for it.

refs.quote: "I know it is."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the final sentence of the passage?

options.text: It confirms that Agnes has decided to remain permanently on the island rather than return to the mainland.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The sentence shows her missing one ferry and standing at a turn in the path; a permanent decision is not stated or implied.

options.text: It reverses the plan laid out in the opening by having Agnes linger at the turn toward the house she was told to avoid.
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening establishes the instruction not to go up to the house and the implied four o'clock return; the ending has her stand at the path to the house and let the ferry go, recasting the errand.

options.text: It demonstrates that Agnes has forgiven Pell for accepting a boat that was worth far more than he paid for it.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The sentence concerns Agnes's relation to the house and the ferry, not to Pell; forgiveness is never at issue.

options.text: It suggests that Agnes has become too distressed by the sale to make her way back along the shingle to the slip.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Her lingering is described as having 'the time now,' a release rather than paralysis; the stones no longer resist her.

items.stem: The observation that the Linnet "looked smaller than Agnes remembered, the way the island did, the way the dock did; only the sky had kept its size" ([[r1]]) most directly conveys that Agnes

options.text: has grown away from a place that once seemed to fill her whole world
options.label: correct
options.why: Everything human-scaled has shrunk relative to her memory while the sky has not, a conventional sign of a returning adult's estrangement; the city shoes and resisting stones reinforce it.

options.text: has begun to suspect that the boat has been damaged since it was hauled in October
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Takes the shrinking literally as physical change; the boat, island and dock cannot all have shrunk, and the comparison is about memory.

options.text: is relieved to find that the island has not changed since her childhood summers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence registers change in her perception, not sameness, and the passage gives no sign of relief.

options.text: feels oppressed by an island sky that is vaster than anything on the mainland
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The sky's constancy is noted neutrally; no oppression or comparison with the mainland sky appears.

items.stem: The narrator of the passage is best described as

options.text: an omniscient voice who moves freely among the thoughts of Agnes, Pell and Hedda
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Pell's and Hedda's thoughts are never given; Hedda is known only through quoted speech and letters, Pell only through what he says and does.

options.text: a third-person voice confined to Agnes's perceptions and memories of the island
options.label: correct
options.why: The narration reports Agnes's memories ('She remembered Hedda in the stern'), her expectations and her realization, but gives no interior access to others.

options.text: a first-person voice recalling, years later, a morning spent on the island as a girl
options.label: misread_speaker
options.why: The passage uses third person ('Agnes thought') throughout and is not framed as retrospection by Agnes.

options.text: a detached observer who reports only what could be seen and overheard on the shingle
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The narrator reports Agnes's thoughts and memories, which an external observer could not see or hear.

items.stem: Agnes's signing the bill of sale "pressing hard so the pencil would take on the damp paper" ([[r1]]), after learning the true nature of the price, most clearly reveals

options.text: her determination to carry out Hedda's wishes exactly as they were written to Pell
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Captures obedience but misses the force of 'pressing hard,' which carries feeling beyond simple compliance.

options.text: her compliance with an arrangement she resents, the pressure of the pencil carrying what she does not say
options.label: correct
options.why: She completes the sale as instructed, yet the hard pressing follows her recognition that she is 'the hands' of someone else's plan; the gesture holds both obedience and suppressed anger.

options.text: her hope that a firmly written signature will make the sale legally binding against future challenge
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Reads the pressing as a practical legal concern; the passage frames the moment as emotional recognition, not legal caution.

options.text: her sudden affection for Pell, whose loyalty to her grandfather she has only now come to understand
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No affection toward Pell is expressed; she does not answer him in the final paragraph.

items.stem: Pell's setting each stone on the shingle "as if it might be needed again" ([[r1]]) most directly suggests that he

options.text: intends to leave the boat under its tarpaulin on the island rather than use it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The stones are weights for a cover, and nothing indicates his plans for the boat; the detail is about his habit, not the boat's future.

options.text: treats even small objects as part of an order that should not be wasted or discarded
options.label: correct
options.why: Consistent with 'did everything in fours' and 'one, two, three'; his careful, provident handling characterizes a man who also kept an unpaid debt for twenty years without discarding it.

options.text: doubts that the sale will go through and expects to have to cover the boat again
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell proceeds confidently with the sale and has Hedda's letters; the 'as if' signals a habit of care, not expectation of failure.

options.text: is deliberately delaying the transaction in order to prolong his time with Agnes
options.label: wrong_function

items.stem: The limitation of the narrative perspective to Agnes most significantly affects the passage by

options.text: allowing the reader to share her mistaken sense of the price until Pell corrects it
options.label: correct
options.why: Because the reader knows only what Agnes knows, the low price seems an insult or a cheat until the fifth paragraph; the reader undergoes the same recognition she does.

options.text: hiding from the reader the fact that Pell and Hedda have been in correspondence
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell states openly in the third paragraph that Hedda wrote to him; the correspondence is not hidden.

options.text: making Pell appear untrustworthy because his motives are never directly stated
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Pell's motives are unstated internally but he explains them plainly in speech; the passage does not render him untrustworthy.

options.text: presenting Hedda's instructions as cruel because Agnes cannot understand them
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Agnes comes to understand the instructions, and the narration treats Hedda's arrangement with rueful recognition rather than as cruelty.

items.stem: The image of the stones, which roll under Agnes "like something that had not agreed to be walked on" ([[r1]]) and later roll "the same as before" ([[r2]]), contributes to the passage mainly by

options.text: marking a change in Agnes rather than in the island, as her hurry gives way to time
options.label: correct
options.why: The ground is explicitly unchanged ('the same as before'); what differs is that Agnes 'had the time now to let them,' so the repeated image measures her altered relation to the place.

options.text: showing that the island grows more hostile to Agnes as she learns the truth about the sale
options.label: reversal
options.why: The stones do not grow more hostile; they are the same, and Agnes's response to them softens.

options.text: emphasizing that Agnes's city shoes are unsuited to the shingle and slow her progress
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: The shoes are a detail of the first image only; the image's return concerns her inner state, not footwear.

options.text: suggesting that Pell has deliberately arranged the stones to make her walk difficult
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Confuses the shingle with the four tarpaulin stones; the beach stones are natural and Pell has no part in them.

items.stem: Agnes's thought of "the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead for the ferryman" ([[r1]]) frames the sale primarily as

options.text: a theft in which Pell, like the ferryman, takes payment from those who cannot refuse

items.stem: The statement that the money "was so little that it did not change the shape of her hand" ([[r1]]) creates a tone best described as

options.text: bitter, as Agnes openly condemns Pell for exploiting her grandmother's pride
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is flat and physical, not condemnatory; Agnes has already learned that Pell's price was Hedda's design.

options.text: dryly understated, registering the sum's insignificance as a bodily fact
options.label: correct
options.why: Rather than naming anger or disappointment, the narrator measures the money by what it fails to do to a glove, a restrained wryness characteristic of the whole passage.

options.text: tender, as Agnes recognizes the money as a token of Pell's love for her family
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage does not frame the money as a token of love, and Agnes's response is withholding, not tender.

options.text: triumphant, as Agnes realizes the boat has been kept from the open market

items.stem: Which of the following thesis statements offers the most defensible and specific interpretation of the passage?

options.text: Through the recurring image of the shingle and Agnes's silence at the end, the passage shows that she becomes the instrument of an old debt and, in resisting that role, discovers a claim on the island.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names specific techniques (recurring image, final silence) and a complex idea with tension (used, yet discovering belonging), both grounded in the text's opening and closing.

options.text: Through Pell's dialogue and Hedda's letters, the passage shows that older people often manipulate the young, and that such manipulation is always harmful to family relationships.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Generalizes beyond the text to 'older people' and 'always harmful'; the passage treats Hedda's arrangement with more ambivalence.

options.text: Through the description of the boat and the island, the passage shows that Agnes travels to Scarrow, sells the Linnet to Pell for a small sum, and then misses the afternoon ferry.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Summarizes plot rather than interpreting it; no claim about meaning or complexity is made.

options.text: Through the allusion to the ferryman and the sale's low price, the passage shows that Pell is the true owner of the boat and that Agnes comes to accept his superior moral claim to it.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The text never asserts Pell's ownership or moral superiority, and Agnes's final silence toward him does not signal acceptance of such a claim.

items.stem: The passage places Agnes's memory of Hedda at the tiller and of Pell "never once in the boat" ([[r1]]) before Pell's explanation of the debt. This ordering most significantly affects the reader by

options.text: making Pell's account confirm an impression already formed of Hedda's refusal to let go
options.label: correct
options.why: The flashback shows Hedda 'declining to let the boat go anywhere else' and Pell excluded; when Pell then explains she would 'let the boat rot sooner than take money,' the reader recognizes rather than learns.

options.text: creating suspense about whether Pell will reveal that he once stole the boat's engine
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No theft is suggested; the debt is for an engine Pell supplied, and the memory raises no such suspicion.

options.text: interrupting the dialogue so that Agnes's protest about the price loses its force
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The interruption deepens rather than dissipates the protest by giving it a history; her objection is not undercut.

options.text: establishing that Agnes remembers the island accurately and so can judge the fair value
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The memory concerns relationships, not valuation; the passage has already settled that the boat is worth more than the price.

options.why: Pell's slowness is characteristic ('did everything in fours'), and nothing in his conduct or speech expresses resentment; he later acts with loyalty to Hedda.

options.text: Agnes's physical weakness compared with a man hardened by sixty years of weather
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Reads the scene as a test of strength; the stones are not described as heavy, and the contrast concerns tempo and manner, not capability.

options.text: Pell's refusal to acknowledge Agnes as the rightful seller of her grandmother's boat
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell immediately recognizes her as 'Hedda's girl' and proceeds with the sale; he does not dispute her role, though he knows Hedda set the terms.

refs.quote: he did not help her, and he did not hurry

evidence_quotes: he did not help her, and he did not hurry

items.stem: A student claims that Hedda controls the sale despite her absence from the island. Which of the following sentences of commentary most clearly links the phrase "arranged the whole morning from under a blanket" ([[r1]]) to that claim?

options.text: The sentence shows that Agnes resents being sent into the wind, which establishes the conflict between the two generations of the family.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Shifts focus from Hedda's control to Agnes's resentment and generational conflict, which the quoted phrase does not itself address.

options.text: The sentence describes Hedda lying in bed at the home, which proves she is too ill to travel to the island herself to sell the boat.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Explains Hedda's absence rather than her control; it restates the circumstance without connecting to the claim's main point.

options.text: The sentence pairs a verb of command with an image of confinement, showing that Hedda's authority survives the loss of her mobility.
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly connects the evidence ('arranged' against 'under a blanket') to the claim about control despite absence; the passage supports it with Hedda's letters to Pell and instructions to Agnes.

options.text: The sentence uses the word 'blanket' to suggest that Hedda is hiding something from Agnes, which the reader learns is the debt owed to Pell.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Over-reads 'blanket' as concealment; the text uses it for physical confinement, and the hidden debt is Pell's revelation, not the point of this phrase.

refs.quote: arranged the whole morning from under a blanket

evidence_quotes: a woman who had arranged the whole morning from under a blanket
She wrote me you were coming. She wrote me what to pay.

items.stem: The placement of Pell's reply "I know it is." ([[r1]]) immediately after Agnes's protest serves primarily to

options.text: show that Pell has been shamed by Agnes into reconsidering the sum he has named
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell does not alter the price; his agreement is calm and the sum remains unchanged through the signing.

options.text: reveal that Pell doubts whether Hedda truly intended the boat to be sold to him
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in Pell's words suggests doubt about Hedda's intent; he cites her letters as authoritative.

options.text: suggest that Agnes has inherited her grandmother's skill at bargaining for a fair price
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The exchange ends bargaining rather than displaying it, and Hedda is shown refusing money, not bargaining for it.

options.text: signal that the price is not a matter of the boat's value, before the reason is given
options.label: correct
options.why: By conceding her point at once, Pell removes value from the dispute; the reader is left with an unexplained gap that the fifth paragraph fills.

refs.quote: "I know it is."

evidence_quotes: "That boat is worth ten times that," she said. "You know it is." "I know it is."
"There isn't a price to argue."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the final sentence of the passage?

options.text: It demonstrates that Agnes has forgiven Pell for accepting a boat that was worth far more than he paid for it.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The sentence concerns Agnes's relation to the house and the ferry, not to Pell; forgiveness is never at issue.

options.text: It confirms that Agnes has decided to remain permanently on the island rather than return to the mainland.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The sentence shows her missing one ferry and standing at a turn in the path; a permanent decision is not stated or implied.

options.text: It reverses the plan laid out in the opening by having Agnes linger at the turn toward the house she was told to avoid.
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening establishes the instruction not to go up to the house and the implied four o'clock return; the ending has her stand at the path to the house and let the ferry go, recasting the errand.

options.text: It suggests that Agnes has become too distressed by the sale to make her way back along the shingle to the slip.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Her lingering is described as having 'the time now,' a release rather than paralysis; the stones no longer resist her.

evidence_quotes: she stood for a while and let the four o'clock leave without her
She had been told not to go up to the house.
you caught the four o'clock back

items.stem: The observation that the Linnet "looked smaller than Agnes remembered, the way the island did, the way the dock did; only the sky had kept its size" ([[r1]]) most directly conveys that Agnes

options.text: has begun to suspect that the boat has been damaged since it was hauled in October
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Takes the shrinking literally as physical change; the boat, island and dock cannot all have shrunk, and the comparison is about memory.

options.text: is relieved to find that the island has not changed since her childhood summers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence registers change in her perception, not sameness, and the passage gives no sign of relief.

options.text: has grown away from a place that once seemed to fill her whole world
options.label: correct
options.why: Everything human-scaled has shrunk relative to her memory while the sky has not, a conventional sign of a returning adult's estrangement; the city shoes and resisting stones reinforce it.

options.text: feels oppressed by an island sky that is vaster than anything on the mainland
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The sky's constancy is noted neutrally; no oppression or comparison with the mainland sky appears.

refs.quote: only the sky had kept its size

evidence_quotes: she looked smaller than Agnes remembered, the way the island did, the way the dock did; only the sky had kept its size
in city shoes, the stones rolling under her like something that had not agreed to be walked on

items.stem: In the sixth paragraph, the description of the mainland as "a gray line with the home somewhere on it, a window, a bed" ([[r1]]) functions primarily to

options.text: explain why Agnes has chosen to settle on the mainland instead of returning to live on the island
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Wrong function: the image locates Hedda, not Agnes; the passage never addresses why Agnes lives on the mainland.

options.text: narrow from a distant horizon to a single bed, locating the scene's hidden author at a remove
options.label: correct
options.why: The syntax moves from 'gray line' to 'window' to 'bed' to 'a woman who had arranged the whole morning,' using the setting to place Hedda both far away and in control.

options.text: contrast the mainland's comfortable prosperity with the island's poverty, neglect, and slow decline
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Unsupported: the image concerns distance and confinement, not any economic contrast between mainland and island.

options.text: suggest that Hedda has been forgotten by the mainland, her bed lost among indifferent, distant windows
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Misreads the image: the passage presents Hedda as the controlling source of the morning, not as forgotten or neglected.

refs.quote: a gray line with the home somewhere on it

evidence_quotes: Across the water the mainland was a gray line with the home somewhere on it, a window, a bed, a woman who had arranged the whole morning from under a blanket

items.stem: The narrator of the passage is best described as

options.text: an omniscient voice who moves freely among the thoughts of Agnes, Pell and Hedda
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Pell's and Hedda's thoughts are never given; Hedda is known only through quoted speech and letters, Pell only through what he says and does.

options.text: a first-person voice recalling, years later, a morning spent on the island as a girl
options.label: misread_speaker
options.why: The passage uses third person ('Agnes thought') throughout and is not framed as retrospection by Agnes.

options.text: a detached observer who reports only what could be seen and overheard on the shingle
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The narrator reports Agnes's thoughts and memories, which an external observer could not see or hear.

options.text: a third-person voice confined to Agnes's perceptions and memories of the island
options.label: correct
options.why: The narration reports Agnes's memories ('She remembered Hedda in the stern'), her expectations and her realization, but gives no interior access to others.

evidence_quotes: She remembered Hedda in the stern with the tiller under her arm
Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.
Agnes knew who.

items.stem: Agnes's signing the bill of sale "pressing hard so the pencil would take on the damp paper" ([[r1]]), after learning the true nature of the price, most clearly reveals

options.text: her worry that a lightly written signature might later let the sale be challenged and undone in law
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Literal for figurative: treats the pressing as legal caution, when the moment is emotional recognition.

options.text: her compliance with an arrangement she resents, the pressure of the pencil carrying what she does not say
options.label: correct
options.why: She completes the sale as instructed, yet the hard pressing follows her recognition that she is 'the hands' of someone else's plan; the gesture holds both obedience and suppressed anger.

options.text: her determination to carry out Hedda's wishes exactly as they had been set down in the letter to Pell
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Too narrow: captures obedience but misses that 'pressing hard' carries unspoken feeling beyond simple compliance.

options.text: her sudden warmth toward Pell, whose quiet loyalty to her grandfather she has only now come to grasp
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Unsupported: no affection toward Pell is expressed, and she does not answer him afterward.

refs.quote: pressing hard so the pencil would take on the damp paper

evidence_quotes: sent her granddaughter to stand in the wind and be the hands of it
Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.
pressing hard so the pencil would take on the damp paper

items.stem: Pell's setting each stone on the shingle "as if it might be needed again" ([[r1]]) most directly suggests that he

options.text: intends to leave the boat under its tarpaulin on the island rather than use it
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The stones are weights for a cover, and nothing indicates his plans for the boat; the detail is about his habit, not the boat's future.

options.text: doubts that the sale will go through and expects to have to cover the boat again
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell proceeds confidently with the sale and has Hedda's letters; the 'as if' signals a habit of care, not expectation of failure.

options.text: treats even small objects as part of an order that should not be wasted or discarded
options.label: correct
options.why: Consistent with 'did everything in fours' and 'one, two, three'; his careful, provident handling characterizes a man who also kept an unpaid debt for twenty years without discarding it.

options.text: is deliberately delaying the transaction in order to prolong his time with Agnes
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: His slowness is habitual throughout; no interest in prolonging contact with Agnes is shown.

refs.quote: as if it might be needed again

evidence_quotes: Osk Pell did everything in fours.
setting each on the shingle as if it might be needed again
He never paid it and I never asked

items.stem: The limitation of the narrative perspective to Agnes most significantly affects the passage by

options.text: allowing the reader to share her mistaken sense of the price until Pell corrects it
options.label: correct
options.why: Because the reader knows only what Agnes knows, the low price seems an insult or a cheat until the fifth paragraph; the reader undergoes the same recognition she does.

options.text: making Pell appear untrustworthy because his motives are never directly stated
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Pell's motives are unstated internally but he explains them plainly in speech; the passage does not render him untrustworthy.

options.text: hiding from the reader the fact that Pell and Hedda have been in correspondence
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell states openly in the third paragraph that Hedda wrote to him; the correspondence is not hidden.

options.text: presenting Hedda's instructions as cruel because Agnes cannot understand them
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Agnes comes to understand the instructions, and the narration treats Hedda's arrangement with rueful recognition rather than as cruelty.

evidence_quotes: It was less than her train fare had been.
"That's the price. She's paying the debt. She wants it to look like a sale."
Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.

items.stem: The image of the stones, which roll under Agnes "like something that had not agreed to be walked on" ([[r1]]) and later roll "the same as before" ([[r2]]), contributes to the passage mainly by

options.text: marking a change in Agnes rather than in the island, as her hurry gives way to time
options.label: correct
options.why: The ground is explicitly unchanged ('the same as before'); what differs is that Agnes 'had the time now to let them,' so the repeated image measures her altered relation to the place.

options.text: showing that the island grows more hostile to Agnes as she learns the truth about the sale
options.label: reversal
options.why: The stones do not grow more hostile; they are the same, and Agnes's response to them softens.

options.text: emphasizing that Agnes's city shoes are unsuited to the shingle and slow her progress
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: The shoes are a detail of the first image only; the image's return concerns her inner state, not footwear.

options.text: suggesting that Pell has deliberately arranged the stones to make her walk difficult
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Confuses the shingle with the four tarpaulin stones; the beach stones are natural and Pell has no part in them.

refs.quote: like something that had not agreed to be walked on
the stones rolled the same as before

evidence_quotes: the stones rolling under her like something that had not agreed to be walked on
the stones rolled the same as before, but she had the time now to let them

items.stem: Agnes's thought of "the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead for the ferryman" ([[r1]]) frames the sale primarily as

options.text: a ritual that Agnes performs correctly because her grandmother has instructed her in it
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The allusion registers confusion ('the stories never said what happened'), not correct performance of a ritual.

options.text: a passage toward Hedda's death, with roles so inverted that Agnes cannot tell who pays whom
options.label: correct
options.why: The burial coin ties the sale to Hedda's approaching end, and the twist that the ferryman pays captures Agnes's realization that she is not the seller she thought.

options.text: a theft in which Pell, like the ferryman, takes payment from those who cannot refuse
options.label: reversal
options.why: Agnes notes that in this case the ferryman is the one paying; the allusion is inverted, not applied straightforwardly to Pell as taker.

options.text: a superstition of the island that Agnes, as a mainlander, no longer takes seriously
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The story is a classical myth, not an island custom, and Agnes's thought treats it seriously as a frame for her situation.

refs.quote: the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead

evidence_quotes: how the stories never said what happened if the ferryman was the one who paid
Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.

items.stem: The statement that the money "was so little that it did not change the shape of her hand" ([[r1]]) creates a tone best described as

options.text: bitter, as Agnes openly condemns Pell for exploiting her grandmother's pride
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is flat and physical, not condemnatory; Agnes has already learned that Pell's price was Hedda's design.

options.text: dryly understated, registering the sum's insignificance as a bodily fact
options.label: correct
options.why: Rather than naming anger or disappointment, the narrator measures the money by what it fails to do to a glove, a restrained wryness characteristic of the whole passage.

options.text: tender, as Agnes recognizes the money as a token of Pell's love for her family
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage does not frame the money as a token of love, and Agnes's response is withholding, not tender.

options.text: triumphant, as Agnes realizes the boat has been kept from the open market
options.label: reversal
options.why: There is no triumph; Agnes has just recognized she was used, and the sentence deflates rather than elevates.

refs.quote: it did not change the shape of her hand

evidence_quotes: Pell counted the money into her glove, and it was so little that it did not change the shape of her hand
It was less than her train fare had been.

items.stem: Which of the following thesis statements offers the most defensible and specific interpretation of the passage?

options.text: Through the recurring image of the shingle and Agnes's silence at the end, the passage shows that she becomes the instrument of an old debt and, in resisting that role, discovers a claim on the island.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names specific techniques (recurring image, final silence) and a complex idea with tension (used, yet discovering belonging), both grounded in the text's opening and closing.

options.text: Through the description of the boat and the island, the passage shows that Agnes travels to Scarrow, sells the Linnet to Pell for a small sum, and then misses the afternoon ferry.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Summarizes plot rather than interpreting it; no claim about meaning or complexity is made.

options.text: Through Pell's dialogue and Hedda's letters, the passage shows that older people often manipulate the young, and that such manipulation is always harmful to family relationships.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Generalizes beyond the text to 'older people' and 'always harmful'; the passage treats Hedda's arrangement with more ambivalence.

options.text: Through the allusion to the ferryman and the sale's low price, the passage shows that Pell is the true owner of the boat and that Agnes comes to accept his superior moral claim to it.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The text never asserts Pell's ownership or moral superiority, and Agnes's final silence toward him does not signal acceptance of such a claim.

evidence_quotes: sent her granddaughter to stand in the wind and be the hands of it
the stones rolled the same as before, but she had the time now to let them
Agnes did not answer.

items.stem: The passage places Agnes's memory of Hedda at the tiller and of Pell "never once in the boat" ([[r1]]) before Pell's explanation of the debt. This ordering most significantly affects the reader by

options.text: creating suspense about whether Pell will reveal that he once stole the boat's engine
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No theft is suggested; the debt is for an engine Pell supplied, and the memory raises no such suspicion.

options.text: interrupting the dialogue so that Agnes's protest about the price loses its force
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The interruption deepens rather than dissipates the protest by giving it a history; her objection is not undercut.

options.text: establishing that Agnes remembers the island accurately and so can judge the fair value
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The memory concerns relationships, not valuation; the passage has already settled that the boat is worth more than the price.

options.text: making Pell's account confirm an impression already formed of Hedda's refusal to let go
options.label: correct
options.why: The flashback shows Hedda 'declining to let the boat go anywhere else' and Pell excluded; when Pell then explains she would 'let the boat rot sooner than take money,' the reader recognizes rather than learns.

refs.quote: never once in the boat

evidence_quotes: not steering so much as declining to let the boat go anywhere else
She remembered Osk Pell on the dock those summers, never once in the boat. Never once.
"She'd have let the boat rot sooner than take money from me."
